newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair announces core of new cabinet.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair announces core of new cabinet.

text.p: Britain's new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair announced the core of his cabinet on Friday as aides promised he would "hit the ground running."
Gordon Brown was named Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister), Robin Cook foreign secretary, John Prescott deputy prime minister and Margaret Beckett trade secretary.
David Blunkett, Britain's first blind cabinet minister, became education secretary and Jack Straw was appointed Home Secretary (interior minister).
Derry Irvine, the lawyer who took both Blair and his wife Cherie Booth on as trainee or pupil barristers 20 years ago, was named Lord Chancellor, the government's top legal post.
There were few surprises among the names of the top seven posts detailed in the government's first announcement after its stunning landslide victory in Thursday's election.
But with more than 400 Labour members of parliament now jostling to get a foothold on the ladder of power, the next few days will bring disappointment or joy for many.
Blair, enjoying his triumph after leading Labour out of 18 years in the political wilderness, will announce the rest of his ministerial team over the weekend.
The choice of his cabinet presents him with his first headache of government because of a clash between Labour party rules and British law.

The cabinet is limited by law to 22 paid posts but party rules mean Blair should include all those who were voted onto the 19-member so-called "shadow cabinet" which harried the Conservatives while Labour was in opposition.
Add in the prime minister, his deputy, the leader of the House of Lords and the Lord Chancellor and the total reaches 23.

Add in at least four key members of Blair's team -- five with campaign supremo Peter Mandelson -- who were not elected to the shadow cabinet, whose composition often reflects internal party politics rather than ability, and the list hits 27 or 28.
The size of Labout' majority immediately dashed the admittedly slim Liberal Democrat hopes of a minor government role.
A senior aide said no other parties would join the government, dismissing suggestions Blair could decide to break the political mould and bring the main minority party on board.
But there will be anxious hours now for Labour ministerial hopefuls. One of those at risk was reassured.
Clare Short, moved from transport to overseas development before the election after speaking loosely of tax rises and the legalisation of cannabis, was tipped for the cabinet by an aide.
But there was a pointed refusal to confirm Michael Meacher, one of the few Labour members with experience of government but who has been at odds with Blair's modernisation of the party.
Those who seemed assured of post included social security spokeswoman Harriet Harman and health spokesman Chris Smith, the only member of parliament to have declared his homosexuality openly,
Scottish spokesman George Robertson was also well-placed as was Labour's chief parliamentary business manager, Donald Dewar.
Northern Ireland spokeswoman Marjorie Mowlam was almost certain to retain her job, particularly after her public image was boosted by a battle to recover from a brain tumour.

Deputy economics spokesman Alistair Darling, one of a group of bright Scottish lawyers at the top of the party, was also tipped for the top along with public services spokesman Derek Foster, who was publicly promised a cabinet job before the election.

Others in the running were environment spokeman Frank Dobson, agriculture spokesman Gavin Strang, shadow leader of the House of Commons Ann Taylor, transport spokesman Andrew Smith, national heritage spokesman Jack Cunningham, Welsh affairs spokesman Ron Davies, defence spokesman David Clark, spokesman for the disabled Tom Clarke and campaign supremo Peter Mandelson.
Unfortunately for some of them, nine into six will not go.
